lessons.title: Forces as vectors

blocks.text: Split one force

A force at angle θ above the horizontal splits into F cos θ along the horizontal and F sin θ along the vertical. For 10 kN at 30°, that is 10 cos 30° = 8.66 kN across and 10 sin 30° = 5.00 kN up. The two components together act exactly as the original force does, so a free-body diagram may show either description, never both.
Read a slope, not an angle

Drawings often give a slope instead of an angle. A line rising 3 for every 4 across has length 5 on the same scale, so cos θ = 4/5 and sin θ = 3/5 without a calculator. A 5 kN pull along it has components 4 kN across and 3 kN up. Scale the force by the matching side of the triangle over its long side.
Add components, not sizes

Forces in different directions do not add like plain numbers. Sum the x-components, sum the y-components, then combine them: R = √(Rx² + Ry²). The 3 kN and 4 kN forces give Rx = 3 kN, Ry = 4 kN and R = 5 kN. Only when two forces share a line of action does their sum reach 7 kN.
Close the force polygon

A point is in equilibrium when ΣFx = 0 and ΣFy = 0. Drawn tip to tail, its forces then close into a polygon with no gap. The third force must match the resultant of the other two in size and point exactly opposite it; here that means 10 kN. Press Play to slide the arrows tip to tail: with a 7 kN third force a gap remains.

lessons.orientation: Resolve forces into components and add them on a free-body diagram.

lessons.title: Turning effect: moments

blocks.text: Force times perpendicular distance

A moment measures how strongly a force turns a body about a point: M = F × d, where d is the perpendicular distance from the point to the force's line of action. A 150 N push at right angles on a spanner, 0.3 m from the bolt, gives 150 × 0.3 = 45 N·m. This course counts anticlockwise moments as positive.
An angled push does less

Only the part of the force at right angles to the arm turns it. At 30°, the perpendicular distance from the bolt to the line of action is 0.3 sin 30° = 0.15 m, so M = 150 × 0.15 = 22.5 N·m. Equivalently, take the perpendicular component 150 sin 30° = 75 N and multiply by the full 0.3 m.
A force through the pivot

A force whose line of action passes through the point has no lever arm, so its moment about that point is zero, whatever the size of the force. Pulling along a spanner never loosens a nut. Engineers exploit this when they take moments about a point where an unknown force acts: that unknown drops out of the equation.
Balance clockwise against anticlockwise

A body at rest on a pivot has zero net moment. The 300 N child 2 m left turns the plank anticlockwise with 600 N·m; a 400 N child must supply 600 N·m clockwise, so sits 600/400 = 1.5 m right. Add moments with their signs. The sizes of the forces alone do not decide the balance.

lessons.title: Reactions of a supported beam

blocks.text: Take moments about a support

Take moments about a support and its unknown reaction drops out. About A, the 12 kN load acts 2 m away, clockwise, and R_B acts 6 m away, anticlockwise: 6R_B = 12 × 2, so R_B = 4 kN. The support nearer the load always carries the larger share of it.
Then sum the vertical forces

With R_B known, vertical equilibrium gives the other reaction: R_A + R_B = 12 kN, so R_A = 8 kN. Check with moments about B: 6R_A = 12 × 4 = 48. One rigid body gives these equations, ΣF = 0 and ΣM = 0, and a pin and roller under vertical loads leave exactly two unknowns for them to find.
A spread load acts at its centre

For reactions, a uniform load can be replaced by its total, intensity times length, acting at the middle of the loaded length. Here 4 kN/m over 3 m is 12 kN at x = 1.5 m. Moments about the left support give 6R_B = 12 × 1.5, so R_B = 3 kN and R_A = 9 kN. The replacement works for reactions; inside the loaded length the bending is different.
A load beyond the support

When a load overhangs a support, the far support must pull down. About A: 4R_B = 10 × 6, so R_B = 15 kN upward, more than the load itself. Then R_A = 10 − 15 = −5 kN: the left support holds the beam down. A support built only to push would let that end lift off.

lessons.title: Trusses: the method of joints

blocks.text: Start at a joint with two unknowns

A truss is a frame of straight members pinned at joints and loaded only at joints, so each member carries a pure push or pull along its length. The method of joints isolates one joint at a time. At C, two unknown member forces meet. By symmetry they are equal, and their vertical components must hold up 12 kN: 2F × 1.5/2.5 = 12, so F = 10 kN.
Tension or compression

A tension member pulls on its joints and gets longer; a compression member pushes on them and gets shorter. The sloping members here push down and outward on A and B, so they are in compression. The bottom chord AB stops the feet spreading by pulling inward on both joints, so it is in tension. A tie can be a slim rod; a strut must also resist buckling.
Joint A gives the tie force

With no horizontal load, the pin at A supplies no horizontal reaction, so the horizontal components at A must cancel. Member AC pushes on A with a horizontal component of 10 × 2/2.5 = 8 kN outward, so AB must pull 8 kN inward. The vertical component, 10 × 1.5/2.5 = 6 kN, matches the 6 kN reaction at A.
Members that carry nothing

At D, members AD and DB lie on one line and no load is applied. Vertical equilibrium at D involves only DC, so DC carries no force. The rule: where two collinear members meet a third at an unloaded joint, the third is a zero-force member. It is not useless. Hang the load from D instead and DC becomes the member that carries it up to the apex.

lessons.title: Stress, strain and stiffness

blocks.text: Stress is force per area

Stress is internal force per unit area: σ = F/A. Engineers use newtons per square millimetre, which equal megapascals. 20 kN is 20,000 N; spread over 400 mm² it gives 50 MPa. Stress, not force, decides whether a material yields: a thicker bar carries the same force at lower stress.
Strain is stretch per length

Strain is extension divided by original length, ε = δ/L, a pure number. In the elastic range stress and strain are proportional, σ = Eε. Here ε = 50/200,000 = 0.00025, so the 2,000 mm bar stretches 0.00025 × 2,000 = 0.5 mm: too small to see, easy to measure with a strain gauge.
Young's modulus is the slope

Young's modulus E is the slope of the straight, elastic part of the stress–strain curve. Aluminium alloy has E ≈ 70 GPa and steel about 200 GPa, so at equal stress aluminium strains 200/70 ≈ 2.9 times as much. Stiffness and strength are different properties: this alloy yields at about the stress mild steel does, yet stretches far more on the way.
Past the yield point

Below the yield stress, unloading retraces the straight line and the bar recovers its length. Beyond yield, planes of atoms slip; unloading follows a line parallel to the elastic one and leaves a permanent strain. The bar still holds load until stress reaches the ultimate strength, where it necks and then fractures. Design keeps working stresses below yield.

lessons.title: Factor of safety and sizing

blocks.text: Margin against yield

The factor of safety compares the stress that causes failure with the stress in service: FoS = σ_yield/σ_working. 40 kN on 400 mm² is 100 MPa; with a 250 MPa yield stress the factor is 2.5. The margin covers loads larger than expected, weaker material, corrosion and the simplifications in the calculation itself.
Size the section

Design runs the calculation backwards. The allowable stress is σ_yield/FoS = 250/2 = 125 MPa, so the area must be at least 60,000/125 = 480 mm². Any section with less area works harder than allowed; any with more is safe but heavier and dearer.
Choose from stock

Members come in stock sizes, so the choice is the smallest available section that meets the required area. A 20 mm square gives 400 mm², too little; a 25 mm square gives 625 mm². Its stress falls to 96 MPa and its factor of safety rises to about 2.6. Rounding up is normal practice.
Stiffness can govern

Strength is not the only check. A member safe against yield may still stretch, sag or vibrate too much. At 96 MPa the 3 m tie lengthens 96/200,000 × 3,000 = 1.44 mm. If the connection it serves tolerates only 1 mm, stiffness governs and the section must grow beyond what strength alone requires.

lessons.orientation: Size a member for strength with a margin, then check that it is stiff enough.

lessons.title: Shear force and bending moment

blocks.text: Cut the beam

Cut the beam anywhere and the left piece must still balance. The shear force V at the cut is the sum of vertical forces to its left, upward positive. Left of the load only R_A = 8 kN acts, so V = +8 kN; right of it, V = 8 − 12 = −4 kN. A point load makes the shear diagram jump by exactly its size.
Moment peaks under a point load

The bending moment at a cut is the total moment, about the cut, of the forces to its left. Under the load only R_A acts on the left piece, so M = 8 × 2 = 16 kN·m, sagging. Between point loads the moment changes linearly: here it rises from zero at A to its peak under the load and falls back to zero at B.
A uniform load makes a parabola

Under a uniform load the shear falls steadily and the moment curve becomes a parabola. Each reaction is wL/2 = 12 kN. At midspan, the left half has 12 kN up at 4 m from the cut and 12 kN of load acting 2 m from it: M = 12 × 4 − 12 × 2 = 24 kN·m. That is the standard result M_max = wL²/8.
Where the moment peaks

The slope of the moment diagram equals the shear force: dM/dx = V. Where V changes sign, from positive to negative, the moment stops rising and starts falling, so its peak sits where the shear passes through zero. Move the section marker and compare the two readings: the largest moment lines up with the shear diagram's crossing.

lessons.title: Bending stress and the I-beam

blocks.text: Stress grows from the neutral axis

Bending stretches one face of a beam and squashes the other. Stress is zero on the neutral axis and grows linearly with distance y from it: σ = My/I. For a 100 × 200 mm section, I = 100 × 200³/12 = 66.7 × 10⁶ mm⁴, and the outer fibres sit 100 mm out, so σ = 20 × 10⁶ × 100/(66.7 × 10⁶) = 30 MPa.
Depth matters most

Same material, same area, different orientation. Laid flat, I = 200 × 100³/12 = 16.7 × 10⁶ mm⁴, a quarter of before, while the outer fibres move in to 50 mm. The stress doubles to 60 MPa. Depth enters I as a cube, which is why floor joists stand on edge.
The second moment of area

The second moment of area I measures how far a section's material sits from the neutral axis: each small area is weighted by the square of its distance. For a rectangle, I = bh³/12. For 60 × 100 mm that is 5 × 10⁶ mm⁴. Double the width and I doubles; double the depth and it rises eightfold.
Put material far from the axis

Material near the neutral axis carries little stress and adds little to I. An I-section moves it into flanges at the top and bottom. This one uses 3,080 mm² against 20,000 mm² for the solid 100 × 200 mm rectangle, 15% of the material, yet keeps 31% of its I. Per kilogram of steel it is about twice as effective in bending.

lessons.orientation: Use σ = My/I and see why depth and flanges make a beam efficient.

lessons.title: Deflection and stiffness

blocks.text: Tip deflection

An end-loaded cantilever deflects δ = PL³/3EI at its tip. Work in base units: P = 3,000 N, L³ = 8 m³, E = 200 × 10⁹ Pa and I = 2 × 10⁻⁶ m⁴, so EI = 400,000 N·m² and δ = 24,000/1,200,000 = 0.02 m, or 20 mm. The product EI, the flexural rigidity, joins material and shape.
Length is cubed

Length enters as a cube. Doubling L makes the tip deflection 2³ = 8 times larger, 160 mm here, because the longer arm both raises the bending moment and gives more length over which the curvature adds up. Long spans are usually governed by stiffness well before strength.
Material and section

Swap steel for aluminium and E falls from 200 to 70 GPa, so deflection rises by 200/70 ≈ 2.9 for the same section. To match steel, an aluminium beam needs 2.9 times the I, usually from a deeper section. Because I grows with depth cubed, a section about 42% deeper is enough, at roughly half the weight of the steel.
Stiffness is load per deflection

Stiffness is load per unit deflection. For an end-loaded cantilever, k = P/δ = 3EI/L³. For the 2 m steel arm, 3 × 400,000/8 = 150,000 N/m, or 150 kN/m: each kilonewton at the tip moves it about 6.7 mm. A diving board is designed for low stiffness; a machine-tool arm for very high stiffness.

lessons.orientation: Predict how far a cantilever bends with δ = PL³/3EI and trade length, material and shape.

lessons.title: Levers and pulleys

blocks.text: Trade distance for force

Mechanical advantage is output force divided by input force. For a lever balanced about its fulcrum, effort × effort arm = load × load arm, so MA = effort arm/load arm = 1.2/0.2 = 6. The hand moves six times as far as the load. The lever trades distance for force; it creates no energy.
Effort and the three classes

Effort = load × load arm/effort arm = 900 × 0.2/1.2 = 150 N. Halve the handle to 0.6 m and the effort doubles. A wheelbarrow, with the load between wheel and handles, is a second-class lever and also gains force. Tweezers and the forearm put the effort in the middle: third-class levers that give up force for speed and reach.
Strands share the load

In a block and tackle one continuous rope runs over several pulleys. Each strand supporting the moving block carries the same tension, so n strands share the load: effort = load/n. Four strands hold 800 N with 200 N in the rope. Count only the strands attached to, or running round, the moving block.
Work in equals work out

Raising the block 0.5 m shortens each of the 4 strands by 0.5 m, so 2 m of rope passes through the hand. Work in, 200 N × 2 m = 400 J, equals work out, 800 N × 0.5 m = 400 J. An ideal machine conserves force × distance; a real one returns less, as the last lesson measures.

lessons.orientation: Trade distance for force with levers and rope systems, and count what it costs.

lessons.title: Gear trains: speed and torque

blocks.text: Teeth set the ratio

Meshing teeth pass the contact point at the same rate, so speed × teeth is the same on both gears. The 60-tooth gear turns 20/60 as fast as the 20-tooth driver: 1,200 × 20/60 = 400 rpm. The gear ratio, driven teeth over driver teeth, is 3 : 1. The larger wheel always turns more slowly.
Torque goes the other way

Power is torque times angular speed, and an ideal mesh passes all of it on. Slow the shaft by a factor of 3 and its torque rises by 3: 10 × 3 = 30 N·m. A gearbox exchanges speed for torque in the same way a lever exchanges distance for force.
Idlers change direction, not ratio

An idler sits between two gears. Its own speed follows the usual rule, 1,200 × 20/30 = 800 rpm, but its tooth count cancels from the overall ratio: 1,200 × 20/30 × 30/60 is still 400 rpm. What changes is direction. Each external mesh reverses rotation, so with two meshes the output turns the same way as the driver. Idlers also bridge a gap between shafts.
Compound trains multiply

In a compound train two gears share a shaft, so the stage ratios multiply: 45/15 × 60/20 = 3 × 3 = 9, and 1,800 rpm becomes 200 rpm. A single pair giving 9 : 1 would need a 135-tooth wheel against a 15-tooth pinion. Two stages fit the same reduction into a much smaller box.

lessons.orientation: Use tooth counts to find speed, torque and direction through simple and compound trains.

lessons.title: Efficiency and power in a drive

blocks.text: Power is torque times angular speed

Rotational power is torque times angular speed, P = Tω, with ω in radians per second. 1,500 rpm is 1,500 × 2π/60 = 157.1 rad/s, so P = 20 × 157.1 ≈ 3,142 W. The rpm-to-rad/s conversion is the step most often missed; leaving it out gives an answer nearly ten times too large.
Losses multiply

Each mesh loses a little power to friction and oil churning, and losses compound: overall efficiency is the product of the stage efficiencies. 0.95 × 0.95 = 0.9025, so 90.25% of the input reaches the output. Every extra stage costs another few per cent; three stages at 95% would deliver about 86%.
Losses cost torque, not ratio

Teeth cannot slip, so the output of a 4 : 1 gearbox still turns at exactly a quarter of the input speed. The missing power shows up as lost torque instead. The ideal output would be 20 × 4 = 80 N·m; at 90% efficiency the shaft delivers 72 N·m.
Size the motor

Size a motor from the useful output. Lifting 2,000 N at 0.5 m/s needs 1,000 W at the hook; at 80% efficiency the motor must supply 1,250 W. A smaller motor can lift the same load, only more slowly. More strands or stages lower the effort but add friction, and the motor still supplies every watt.

lessons.orientation: Track power through a drive, account for losses and size a motor for a hoist.

questions.prompt: A 10 kN force acts at 30° above the horizontal. Find its horizontal component in kN, to two decimal places.
hints: The horizontal side of the triangle is adjacent to the 30° angle.
Adjacent side = hypotenuse × cos θ.
Calculate 10 × cos 30° and round to two decimal places.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Horizontal component = 10 cos 30° = 8.660 kN, which rounds to 8.66 kN. Using sin 30° by mistake gives 5 kN, the vertical component.

questions.prompt: A cable pulls with 5 kN along a line that rises 3 m for every 4 m across. Find the vertical component of the pull in kN.
hints: Find the long side of a triangle with sides 3 and 4.
The vertical component is the force times rise over the long side.
Calculate 5 × 3/5.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The slope triangle 3–4–5 gives sin θ = 3/5, so the vertical component is 5 × 3/5 = 3 kN.

questions.prompt: A pin carries 3 kN acting horizontally and 4 kN acting vertically. Find the magnitude of their resultant in kN.
hints: The forces are at right angles, so their sizes do not simply add.
Use Pythagoras on the summed components.
Calculate √(3² + 4²).

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: R = √(3² + 4²) = √25 = 5 kN. Adding the sizes to get 7 kN treats perpendicular forces as if they were aligned.

questions.prompt: A ring is held by 6 kN acting along +x and 8 kN acting along +y. What magnitude, in kN, must a third force have to keep the ring in equilibrium?
hints: Equilibrium needs the sum of all forces to be zero.
The third force equals the resultant of the other two in size.
Calculate √(6² + 8²).

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The third force must cancel the resultant of the first two: √(6² + 8²) = 10 kN, pointing opposite it.

questions.prompt: Forces of 12 kN along +x and 5 kN along +y act on the pin of a gusset plate. Find the magnitude of their resultant in kN.
hints: Treat the two forces as perpendicular components.
Square each, add, then take the square root.
Calculate √(144 + 25).

questions.prompt: A lamp hangs from two cables. Its free-body diagram isolates the lamp. Which force belongs on that diagram?
hints: Ask which body each force acts on.

acceptedIdeas: The pull of each cable on the lamp
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A free-body diagram shows only forces acting on the isolated body: the lamp's weight and the two cable pulls on it.

choices.label: The pull of each cable on the lamp
The pull of the lamp on the ceiling

questions.prompt: A 150 N force pushes at right angles to a spanner, 0.3 m from the bolt. Find the moment about the bolt in N·m.
hints: The push is already at right angles, so the full distance counts.
Multiply force by perpendicular distance.
Calculate 150 × 0.3.

questions.prompt: The same 150 N force acts 0.3 m from the bolt, but at 30° to the spanner. Find the moment about the bolt in N·m.
hints: Only the component at right angles to the spanner turns it.
That component is F sin θ, where θ is the angle between force and spanner.
Calculate 150 × sin 30° × 0.3.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: M = 150 × 0.3 × sin 30° = 22.5 N·m. Using cos 30° takes the component along the handle, which does not turn it.

questions.prompt: A 200 N force pulls along a spanner's handle, directly away from the bolt, at a point 0.3 m from it. Find its moment about the bolt in N·m.
hints: Sketch the line of action of the force.
Measure the perpendicular distance from the bolt to that line.
Multiply the force by that distance.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The line of action passes through the bolt, so the perpendicular distance and the moment are both zero.

questions.prompt: A 300 N child sits 2 m left of a seesaw's pivot. How far right of the pivot, in metres, must a 400 N child sit for the seesaw to balance?
hints: The two moments about the pivot must be equal and opposite.
Find the left child's moment, then divide by the right child's weight.
Calculate 300 × 2 ÷ 400.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Balance needs 400 × d = 300 × 2 = 600 N·m, so d = 1.5 m.

questions.prompt: A door handle is 0.8 m from the hinges. It is pulled with 40 N at right angles to the door. Find the moment about the hinges in N·m.
hints: The hinge line is the pivot.
The pull is perpendicular, so use the full 0.8 m.
Calculate 40 × 0.8.

questions.prompt: To loosen a tight nut with the least effort, where and how should you push on the spanner?
hints: Moment is force times perpendicular distance. Make that distance as large as you can.

acceptedIdeas: At the end of the handle, at right angles to it
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The largest perpendicular distance gives the largest moment for a given force, and only a push at right angles uses all of it.

questions.prompt: A 6 m beam rests on a pin at A (x = 0) and a roller at B (x = 6 m). It carries 12 kN at x = 2 m. Take moments about A to find the reaction at B in kN.
hints: Taking moments about A removes R_A from the equation.
The load's moment about A must equal R_B's moment about A.
Calculate 12 × 2 ÷ 6.

questions.prompt: For the same 6 m beam with 12 kN at x = 2 m, find the reaction at A in kN.
hints: The two reactions together must carry the whole load.
Use the reaction at B from moments about A, or take moments about B.
Calculate 12 × 4 ÷ 6.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: R_A = 12 − R_B = 12 − 4 = 8 kN. Moments about B confirm it: 12 × 4 ÷ 6 = 8 kN.

questions.prompt: A 6 m beam on supports at x = 0 and x = 6 m carries 4 kN/m over its first 3 m. Find the reaction at the right-hand support in kN.
hints: Replace the spread load by its total acting at the middle of the loaded length.
Take moments about the left support.
Calculate (4 × 3) × 1.5 ÷ 6.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The spread load totals 4 × 3 = 12 kN acting at x = 1.5 m. About the left support: 6R = 12 × 1.5, so R = 3 kN.

questions.prompt: A beam has supports at x = 0 and x = 4 m and a 10 kN load at its free end, x = 6 m. Taking upward as positive, find the reaction at x = 0 in kN.
hints: Find the reaction at x = 4 m first, by moments about x = 0.
Then the two reactions must add to the 10 kN load.
Calculate 10 − 10 × 6 ÷ 4, keeping the sign.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: About x = 0: 4R_B = 10 × 6, so R_B = 15 kN. Then R_A = 10 − 15 = −5 kN: the left support pulls down.

questions.prompt: A 10 m beam on supports at its ends carries 20 kN at x = 3 m and 10 kN at x = 8 m. Find the left reaction in kN.
hints: Take moments about the right-hand support to remove its reaction.
Measure each load's distance from x = 10 m.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: About the right support: 10R_A = 20 × 7 + 10 × 2 = 160, so R_A = 16 kN.

questions.prompt: Name the support that stops a beam moving vertically but lets it slide horizontally and rotate.
hints: One support of a simply supported beam is free to slide so the beam can expand.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A roller support: it pushes at right angles to its surface and nothing more.

questions.prompt: A triangular truss spans 4 m with its apex C 1.5 m above the supports, so each sloping member is 2.5 m long. A 12 kN load hangs from C. Find the size of the force in member AC in kN.
hints: Isolate joint C. Two equal member forces meet there.
Each contributes a vertical component of F × rise/length.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: At C, both sloping members have vertical components of F × 1.5/2.5. Then 2 × 0.6F = 12, so F = 10 kN. Forgetting the second member gives 20 kN.

questions.prompt: In that same truss, is the bottom member AB in tension or compression?
hints: Picture the sloping members spreading under the load. What must AB do to stop the feet moving apart?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Tension: AB pulls inward to stop the supports spreading apart.

questions.prompt: Use joint A of the shallow truss. The 10 kN force in AC acts along a line with run 2 m and rise 1.5 m. Find the force in AB in kN.
hints: The pin at A has no horizontal reaction because no load acts horizontally.
AB must cancel the horizontal component of AC.
Calculate 10 × 2/2.5.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Horizontal balance at A: F_AB = 10 × 2/2.5 = 8 kN, in tension.

questions.prompt: A king-post truss adds a vertical member DC from the middle of the bottom chord, D, up to the apex C. The only load is 12 kN at C. Find the force in DC in kN.
hints: Isolate joint D and list the members meeting there.
AD and DB lie on one straight line; DC is the only member with a vertical component.
Write ΣFy = 0 at D with no load applied there.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: At D, AD and DB are collinear and horizontal and no load acts, so vertical balance leaves DC with no force.

questions.prompt: A triangular truss spans 3 m with its apex 2 m high, so each sloping member is 2.5 m long. A 16 kN load acts at the apex. Find the tension in the bottom member in kN.
hints: Find the sloping member force first, at the apex.
Then use horizontal balance at a support joint.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: At the apex: 2F × 2/2.5 = 16, so F = 10 kN in each sloping member. At a support: tension = 10 × 1.5/2.5 = 6 kN.

questions.prompt: A member pushes outward on the joints at both its ends. What is it in: tension or compression?
hints: Ask whether the member is being stretched or squashed.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Compression: a strut pushes on its joints.

questions.prompt: A steel bar with a cross-section of 400 mm² carries a 20 kN axial pull. Find the stress in MPa.
hints: Convert the load to newtons.
Divide by the area in mm²; 1 N/mm² is 1 MPa.
Calculate 20,000 ÷ 400.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: σ = 20,000 N ÷ 400 mm² = 50 N/mm² = 50 MPa. Leaving the load in kN gives 0.05, a thousand times too small.

questions.prompt: The same bar is 2,000 mm long, and its steel has E = 200 GPa (200,000 MPa). At 50 MPa, how much does it stretch, in mm?
hints: Strain is stress divided by Young's modulus, in the same units.
Stretch is strain times original length.

questions.prompt: An aluminium bar (E = 70 GPa) 1,400 mm long carries a stress of 50 MPa. Find its stretch in mm.
hints: Write E in MPa: 70 GPa is 70,000 MPa.
Strain = stress ÷ E, then multiply by length.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: ε = 50/70,000; δ = 50/70,000 × 1,400 = 1 mm, double the steel bar's stretch over a shorter length.

questions.prompt: A steel bar with yield stress 250 MPa and ultimate strength 400 MPa is loaded to 300 MPa, then unloaded. What happens?
hints: Compare 300 MPa with both strengths.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: 300 MPa is past yield but below the ultimate strength, so the bar survives with a permanent set.

choices.label: It returns to its original length

questions.prompt: A square rod 10 mm × 10 mm carries a 15 kN axial pull. Find the stress in MPa.
hints: Find the cross-sectional area first.
Convert the load to newtons and divide.

questions.prompt: A steel tie (E = 200 GPa) 5 m long works at 100 MPa. Find its stretch in mm.
hints: Convert the length to millimetres.
Strain = stress ÷ E with E in MPa.

questions.prompt: A steel tie with yield stress 250 MPa and area 400 mm² carries 40 kN. Find its factor of safety against yield.
hints: Find the working stress first.
Divide the yield stress by the working stress.

questions.prompt: A tie must carry 60 kN with a factor of safety of 2, using steel that yields at 250 MPa. Find the minimum cross-sectional area in mm².
hints: Divide the yield stress by the factor of safety.
Area = load in newtons ÷ allowable stress.
Calculate 60,000 ÷ 125.

questions.prompt: Square steel bars come with 20, 25 and 30 mm sides. Which side length, in mm, is the smallest that gives at least 480 mm² of area?
hints: Work out the area of each bar.
Discard any below the required area.
Pick the smallest remaining side.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Areas are 400, 625 and 900 mm². 400 mm² is too small, so the 25 mm bar is the lightest that works.

questions.prompt: A 25 mm square steel tie (625 mm²) is 3 m long and carries 60 kN. With E = 200 GPa, find its stretch in mm.
hints: Find the stress in MPa.
Strain = stress ÷ 200,000 MPa; multiply by 3,000 mm.

questions.prompt: A steel with yield stress 355 MPa is used with a factor of safety of 2.5. Find the allowable working stress in MPa.
hints: The factor of safety divides the failure stress.
Allowable = yield ÷ FoS.
Calculate 355 ÷ 2.5.

questions.prompt: A 300 mm² bar of steel that yields at 250 MPa must keep a factor of safety of 1.5. Find the largest axial load it may carry, in kN.
hints: Find the allowable stress.
Load = allowable stress × area, in newtons.
Calculate 300 × 250 ÷ 1.5, then convert to kN.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Allowable stress = 250 ÷ 1.5 MPa; load = 300 × 250 ÷ 1.5 = 50,000 N = 50 kN.

questions.prompt: A 6 m beam on end supports carries 12 kN at x = 2 m, so the reactions are 8 kN at A and 4 kN at B. Find the shear force just to the right of the load, in kN, counting upward forces on the left piece as positive.
hints: Add the vertical forces on the piece to the left of the cut.
Just right of the load, both R_A and the load are on the left piece.
Calculate 8 − 12, keeping the sign.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Left of the cut: +8 kN reaction and −12 kN load, so V = 8 − 12 = −4 kN.

questions.prompt: For the same beam, find the bending moment under the 12 kN load, in kN·m.
hints: Take moments about the cut of the forces on its left.
R_A is the only force to the left, 2 m away.
Calculate 8 × 2.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Only R_A acts left of the cut: M = 8 × 2 = 16 kN·m, sagging.

questions.prompt: An 8 m beam on end supports carries a uniform 3 kN/m along its full length. Find the largest bending moment, in kN·m.
hints: By symmetry the peak is at midspan.
Use M_max = wL²/8, or balance the left half about the cut.
Calculate 3 × 8² ÷ 8.

questions.prompt: Along a simply supported beam, what is the shear force where the bending moment reaches its peak? Answer in one word.
hints: The slope of the moment diagram equals the shear force.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Zero: the moment's slope is the shear, and the slope vanishes at the peak.

questions.prompt: A 3 m cantilever carries 5 kN at its free end. Find the size of the bending moment at the wall, in kN·m.
hints: Cut at the wall and look at the free piece.
Only the end load acts on it.
Calculate 5 × 3.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The load acts 3 m from the wall: M = 5 × 3 = 15 kN·m, hogging.

questions.prompt: A 10 m beam on end supports carries 20 kN at midspan. Find the largest bending moment, in kN·m.
hints: Find the reactions by symmetry.
The peak is under the load.
Calculate 10 × 5.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Each reaction is 10 kN; under the load M = 10 × 5 = 50 kN·m. This is PL/4.

questions.prompt: A solid rectangular beam 100 mm wide and 200 mm deep carries a bending moment of 20 kN·m. Its second moment of area is bh³/12. Find the largest bending stress, in MPa.
hints: Convert the moment to N·mm: 1 kN·m = 10⁶ N·mm.
The outer fibre is half the depth from the neutral axis.

questions.prompt: The same beam is laid flat, 200 mm wide and 100 mm deep, under the same 20 kN·m. Find the largest bending stress, in MPa.
hints: Swap the width and depth in bh³/12.
The outer fibre is now 50 mm from the axis.

questions.prompt: Find the second moment of area of a rectangle 60 mm wide and 100 mm deep about its horizontal centroidal axis, in units of 10⁶ mm⁴.
hints: Use I = bh³/12 with h the depth.
Cube the depth before multiplying by the width.
Calculate 60 × 1,000,000 ÷ 12, then divide by 10⁶.

questions.prompt: An I-section is 200 mm deep with 100 mm wide, 10 mm thick flanges and a 6 mm web. Its I is the outer rectangle minus the two empty side regions: (100 × 200³ − 94 × 180³)/12. Find I in units of 10⁶ mm⁴, to two decimal places.
hints: Each empty region is 47 mm wide; together they are 94 mm wide and 180 mm deep.
Subtract their combined bh³ from the outer rectangle's.
Divide the difference by 12 and by 10⁶.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 100 × 200³ = 800 × 10⁶ and 94 × 180³ = 548.2 × 10⁶; the difference over 12 is 20.98 × 10⁶ mm⁴.

questions.prompt: A square beam 100 mm × 100 mm carries 5 kN·m. Find the largest bending stress in MPa.
hints: Find I for the square with bh³/12.
The outer fibre is 50 mm from the axis.

questions.prompt: Name the line through a bent beam's cross-section where the bending stress is zero.
hints: Fibres on one side are stretched and on the other squashed. What lies between?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The neutral axis, which passes through the centroid of the section.

questions.prompt: A steel cantilever 2 m long (E = 200 GPa, I = 2 × 10⁶ mm⁴) carries 3 kN at its tip. Using δ = PL³/3EI, find the tip deflection in mm.
hints: Convert to N, m, Pa and m⁴: 10⁶ mm⁴ is 10⁻⁶ m⁴.
Compute EI first, then PL³/3EI in metres.
Calculate 3,000 × 2³ ÷ (3 × 400,000), then convert to mm.

questions.prompt: Keep the load and section but double the cantilever's length. By what factor does the tip deflection grow?
hints: Only L changes in PL³/3EI.
Deflection depends on the cube of length.
Calculate 2³.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: δ ∝ L³, so doubling L multiplies δ by 2³ = 8.

questions.prompt: An aluminium cantilever 1 m long (E = 70 GPa, I = 1 × 10⁶ mm⁴) carries 2.1 kN at its tip. Find the tip deflection in mm.
hints: Find EI in N·m².
Apply δ = PL³/3EI with L = 1 m.
Calculate 2,100 ÷ 210,000 and convert to mm.

questions.prompt: For the 2 m steel cantilever (E = 200 GPa, I = 2 × 10⁶ mm⁴), find the tip stiffness k = 3EI/L³ in kN/m.
hints: EI is 400,000 N·m².
Divide 3EI by L³.
Calculate 3 × 400,000 ÷ 8, then convert N/m to kN/m.

questions.prompt: A 2 m steel cantilever (E = 200 GPa) carries 3 kN at its tip, and its deflection is limited to 8 mm. Find the minimum I, in units of 10⁶ mm⁴.
hints: Rearrange δ = PL³/3EI for I.
Keep δ in metres and E in pascals.
Calculate 24,000 ÷ (4.8 × 10⁹), then convert m⁴ to 10⁶ mm⁴.

questions.prompt: Which single change halves a cantilever's tip deflection under the same load?
hints: Look at where each quantity sits in PL³/3EI.

acceptedIdeas: Doubling the second moment of area
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: δ = PL³/3EI, so doubling I halves δ. Doubling L multiplies δ by 8; halving E doubles it.

choices.label: Doubling the second moment of area

questions.prompt: A crowbar is levered over a fulcrum. The hand pushes 1.2 m from the fulcrum and the load sits 0.2 m from it. Find the mechanical advantage.
hints: Mechanical advantage is load force over effort force.
For a balanced lever, that equals the ratio of the arms.
Calculate 1.2 ÷ 0.2.

questions.prompt: With the same crowbar, find the effort in newtons needed to hold a 900 N load.
hints: Moments about the fulcrum must balance.
Calculate 180 ÷ 1.2.

questions.prompt: A pulley system has 4 rope strands supporting the moving block, which carries an 800 N load. Ignoring friction and the block's weight, find the effort in newtons.
hints: The rope tension is the same in every strand.
The supporting strands share the load equally.
Calculate 800 ÷ 4.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Each of the 4 strands carries the rope tension: effort = 800 ÷ 4 = 200 N.

questions.prompt: To lift that load 0.5 m with 4 supporting strands, how many metres of rope must be pulled?
hints: Every supporting strand gets shorter by the lift height.
The rope taken up comes out through the hand.
Calculate 4 × 0.5.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Each strand shortens by 0.5 m: 4 × 0.5 = 2 m.

questions.prompt: In the forearm, the biceps attaches 0.04 m from the elbow, and a 50 N weight is held in the hand 0.32 m from the elbow. Treating the forearm as a weightless horizontal lever, find the biceps force in newtons.
hints: The elbow is the fulcrum.
Balance moments: effort × effort arm = load × load arm.
Calculate 50 × 0.32 ÷ 0.04.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Biceps × 0.04 = 50 × 0.32, so the biceps pulls 16 ÷ 0.04 = 400 N, eight times the weight held.

questions.prompt: A wheelbarrow has its load between the wheel axle and the handles. Which class of lever is it: first, second or third?
hints: Locate the fulcrum first, then see which of load and effort lies between.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Second class: the load sits between the fulcrum and the effort.

questions.prompt: A 20-tooth driver gear turning at 1,200 rpm meshes with a 60-tooth gear. Find the output speed in rpm.
hints: Speed × teeth is equal on both gears.
The bigger gear turns more slowly.
Calculate 1,200 × 20 ÷ 60.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Output speed = 1,200 × 20 ÷ 60 = 400 rpm. Multiplying by 60/20 instead would speed the larger gear up.

questions.prompt: If the 20-tooth driver supplies 10 N·m and the mesh is lossless, find the output torque on the 60-tooth gear in N·m.
hints: An ideal mesh passes on all the power.
Speed falls by the gear ratio, so torque rises by it.
Calculate 10 × 60 ÷ 20.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Torque rises by the ratio 60/20 = 3: 10 × 3 = 30 N·m.

questions.prompt: A 30-tooth idler is placed between the 20-tooth driver, turning at 1,200 rpm, and the 60-tooth output. Find the idler's speed in rpm.
hints: The idler is driven directly by the 20-tooth gear.
Speed × teeth is equal across that mesh.
Calculate 1,200 × 20 ÷ 30.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The idler meshes with the driver: 1,200 × 20 ÷ 30 = 800 rpm. The output still turns at 1,200 × 20 ÷ 60 = 400 rpm.

questions.prompt: A compound train has 15 teeth driving 45, then, on the same shaft, 20 teeth driving 60. The input turns at 1,800 rpm. Find the output speed in rpm.
hints: Find each stage's ratio, driven over driver.
Multiply the stage ratios for a compound train.
Calculate 1,800 ÷ (3 × 3).

questions.prompt: A bicycle's 48-tooth chainring drives a 16-tooth rear sprocket. The pedals turn at 60 rpm. Find the rear wheel's speed in rpm.
hints: The chain carries teeth past both sprockets at the same rate.
Speed × teeth is equal on both.
Calculate 60 × 48 ÷ 16.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: A chain works like a mesh: 60 × 48 ÷ 16 = 180 rpm. Here the smaller sprocket is driven, so it turns faster.

questions.prompt: A 20-tooth driver turns a 60-tooth output through a 30-tooth idler. Compared with the driver, which way does the output turn: same or opposite?
hints: Each pair of meshing external gears turns in opposite senses. Count the meshes.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The same way: each external mesh reverses rotation, and there are two meshes.

questions.prompt: A motor delivers 20 N·m at 1,500 rpm. Find its power output in watts, to the nearest watt.
hints: Convert rpm to radians per second: multiply by 2π and divide by 60.
Power is torque times angular speed.
Calculate 20 × 1,500 × 2π ÷ 60 and round.

questions.prompt: A gearbox has two meshes, each 95% efficient. Find the overall efficiency as a percentage.
hints: Each stage passes on a fraction of what it receives.
Multiply the stage efficiencies as decimals.
Calculate 0.95², then convert to a percentage.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 0.95 × 0.95 = 0.9025, which is 90.25%. Subtracting 5% twice gives 90%, slightly too low.

questions.prompt: A single-stage gearbox with a 4 : 1 reduction is 90% efficient. The input torque is 20 N·m. Find the output torque in N·m.
hints: Start from the ideal torque multiplication.
Losses reduce torque because the speed ratio is fixed by the teeth.
Calculate 20 × 4 × 0.9.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Ideal output 20 × 4 = 80 N·m; with losses 80 × 0.9 = 72 N·m.

questions.prompt: A hoist lifts 2,000 N at 0.5 m/s through a pulley system that is 80% efficient overall. Find the power the motor must supply, in watts.
hints: Useful power is force times speed.
Input power is useful power divided by efficiency.

questions.prompt: A block and tackle with 4 supporting strands is 80% efficient. Find the effort needed to raise a 1,600 N load, in N.
hints: The ideal effort is load divided by the number of strands.
Friction means the real effort is larger: divide by the efficiency too.

questions.prompt: A designer adds a third reduction stage so that the same motor delivers more output torque. What is given up?
hints: Output power can never exceed input power.

acceptedIdeas: Output speed, plus a little extra loss
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: More reduction multiplies torque by slowing the output, and each extra mesh wastes a few more per cent of the power.

choices.label: Output speed, plus a little extra loss

flashcards.back: R = √(9² + 12²) = 15 kN. The minus sign sets the direction, not the size.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: R = √(9² + 12²) = 15 kN. The minus sign sets the direction, not the size.

flashcards.front: A 50 N force acts at right angles to a lever, 0.6 m from its pivot. Find the moment in N·m.

A 5 m beam on end supports carries 15 kN at 1 m from the left support. Find the right reaction in kN.
flashcards.back: Moments about the left support: 5R = 15 × 1, so R = 3 kN.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Moments about the left support: 5R = 15 × 1, so R = 3 kN.

flashcards.front: A 4 m beam on end supports carries 3 kN/m along its whole length. Find each reaction in kN.
flashcards.back: Total load 12 kN, shared equally by symmetry: 6 kN each.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Total load 12 kN, shared equally by symmetry: 6 kN each.

For 10 kN at 30°, that is 10 cos 30° = 8.66 kN across and 10 sin 30° = 5.00 kN up. The two components together act exactly as the original force does, so a free-body diagram may show either description, never both.

A force at angle θ above the horizontal splits into F cos θ along the horizontal and F sin θ along the vertical. For 10 kN at 30°, that is 10 cos 30° = 8.66 kN across and 10 sin 30° = 5.00 kN up. The two components together act exactly as the original force does, so a free-body diagram may show either description, never both.

courseChecks.title: Find your starting point
courseChecks.description: Twelve problems across forces, structures, beams and machines. Find which ideas need attention before you start.

question.prompt: A 26 kN force acts along a line rising 5 m for every 12 m across. Find its vertical component in kN.
A 60 N force acts at right angles to a lever, 0.45 m from the pivot. Find its moment in N·m.
An 8 m beam on end supports carries 16 kN at x = 2 m. Find the reaction at the right-hand support in kN.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Moments about the left support: 8R = 16 × 2, so R = 4 kN.

question.prompt: A triangular truss spans 8 m with its apex 3 m high, so each sloping member is 5 m long. A 24 kN load acts at the apex. Find the size of the force in each sloping member in kN.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: At the apex: 2F × 3/5 = 24, so F = 20 kN, in compression.

question.prompt: A 30 kN axial pull acts on a bar with a 600 mm² cross-section. Find the stress in MPa.
A 400 mm² tie carries 30 kN in steel that yields at 300 MPa. Find its factor of safety against yield.
A 6 m beam on end supports carries 18 kN at midspan. Find the largest bending moment in kN·m.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Each reaction is 9 kN; under the load M = 9 × 3 = 27 kN·m.

question.prompt: A solid rectangular beam 50 mm wide and 100 mm deep carries 2 kN·m. Find the largest bending stress in MPa.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The left load gives +200 × 1.5 = +300 N·m, the right one −150 × 1 = −150 N·m; net +150 N·m.

question.prompt: A 5 m beam has supports at x = 0 and x = 4 m and a 12 kN load at its free end, x = 5 m. Find the upward reaction at x = 4 m in kN.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Moments about x = 0: 4R = 12 × 5, so R = 15 kN.

question.prompt: In a king-post truss the vertical member DC rises from the middle of the bottom chord, D, to the apex C. A 9 kN load hangs from D. Find the tension in DC in kN.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: At D the collinear chords have no vertical component, so DC alone carries the 9 kN up to C.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Total load 8 kN acting 2 m from the wall: M = 8 × 2 = 16 kN·m.

question.prompt: A Warren truss has bottom joints A, D and B 3 m apart and top joints C and E 2 m up, so each diagonal is 2.5 m long. A 16 kN load hangs from D. Find the size of the force in the top member CE in kN.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Each reaction is 8 kN. At A: F_AC × 2/2.5 = 8, so AC = 10 kN compression. At C, CD balances AC vertically (10 kN tension) and CE = 10 × 1.5/2.5 × 2 = 12 kN compression.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: For a rectangle σ = 6M/(bh²). The deep beam has bh² = 3 × 10⁶ mm³, the shallow one 1.5 × 10⁶ mm³, so its stress is twice as high.
